meta.title: ISM Code ↔ NIST CSF 2.0 Crosswalk

targets: ISM Code (IMO Res. A.741(18), as amended)

meta.disclaimer: This is an informational reference for practitioners, not compliance or legal advice. Every row cites its primary source — verify against the current text of each instrument and consult your class society, flag state, or DPA before relying on any mapping for an actual SMS or DOC audit. Standards revise; check the 'last verified' date above before citing.

rows.title: Organizational mission is understood and informs cybersecurity risk management
rows.vesselContext: Cyber risk sits inside the Company's stated Safety Management objectives, not as a bolt-on IT policy separate from the SMS.

rows.title: Risk management objectives are established and agreed to by organizational stakeholders
rows.vesselContext: The DPA's cyber risk appetite should be a stated SMS objective with sign-off, not an assumed default.

rows.title: A cybersecurity supply chain risk management program is established and agreed to by stakeholders
ism: Section 3 (Company Responsibilities — extends to appointed ship managers/vendors)
rows.msc: No direct MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 clause; see IACS UR E27 (out of MVP scope)
rows.vesselContext: Third-party OT vendors (ECDIS/VSAT providers, remote-maintenance contractors) rarely appear in existing SMS vendor-management procedures today.

rows.title: Roles, responsibilities, and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established and communicated
rows.msc: MSC.428(98) — mandate places responsibility on the Company via ISM Section 4/5
rows.vesselContext: The DPA is the natural cyber-risk owner ashore; the Master retains onboard authority — CSF wants this written down explicitly, not assumed from the general DPA/Master roles.

rows.title: Inventories of hardware managed by the organization are maintained
ism: Section 10 (Maintenance of the Ship and Equipment)
rows.msc: MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.3 Annex — shore-side asset inventory (new in Rev.3)
rows.vesselContext: Extend the existing Planned Maintenance System (PMS) equipment register to cover OT/IT — ECDIS, VSAT modem, engine control unit — not just mechanical plant.

rows.title: Inventories of software, services, and systems managed by the organization are maintained
ism: Section 10 (Maintenance of the Ship and Equipment)
rows.msc: MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3/Rev.3 Annex — shore-side asset inventory (new in Rev.3)
rows.vesselContext: Firmware versions and network services (remote-access clients, AIS transponder software) need their own register — most PMS systems only track hardware, not software/service state.

rows.title: Vulnerabilities in assets are identified, validated, and recorded
ism: Section 9 (Reports and Analysis of Non-Conformities — by extension, after the fact)
rows.vesselContext: No ISM clause covers proactive vulnerability scanning. This is the clearest gap between CSF and ISM — most SMSs only capture vulnerabilities reactively, via non-conformity reports filed after something already went wrong.

rows.title: Threats, vulnerabilities, likelihoods, and impacts are used to understand risk and inform prioritization
rows.vesselContext: The cyber risk assessment should feed the same risk register as other operational hazards (grounding, fire, collision) — not sit in a separate standalone "IT risk" document.

rows.title: Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed
rows.vesselContext: Access-control procedures for OT consoles (ECDIS, engine-control HMI) belong in the same shipboard operating procedures as other critical equipment, with shared-account use named as a specific non-conformity risk.

rows.title: Access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations are defined and enforced
rows.vesselContext: Who may log into the VSAT modem or ECDIS admin account should be a documented, version-controlled procedure — like any other SMS-controlled document.

rows.title: The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data-at-rest are protected
rows.msc: No dedicated MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 clause — implied under "Protect"
rows.vesselContext: VDR data, ECDIS chart updates, and passage plans increasingly live on networked storage. Section 11's document-control intent extends naturally here, but almost no SMS says so explicitly.

rows.title: Configuration management practices are established and applied
ism: Section 10 (Maintenance of the Ship and Equipment)
rows.msc: No dedicated MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 clause — implied under "Protect"
rows.vesselContext: Configuration baselines for OT systems (firewall rules, USB port lockdown) fit the same "maintained in a good state of repair" logic Section 10 already applies to machinery.

rows.title: Personnel are provided with cybersecurity awareness and training
rows.msc: MSC.428(98) does not mandate crew training explicitly — a named gap
rows.vesselContext: Cyber-awareness training for crew and officers has a natural home in Section 6, but MSC.428(98) never mandates it directly — companies must read it into the general competency requirement themselves.

rows.title: Networks and network services are monitored to find potentially adverse events
rows.vesselContext: Anomaly-detection findings should route into the same non-conformity / hazardous-occurrence reporting line as any other operational deviation — not a siloed IT log nobody in the SMS ever reads.

rows.title: Computing hardware and software, runtime environments, and their data are monitored
ism: Section 10 (Maintenance of the Ship and Equipment)
rows.vesselContext: Extends PMS condition-monitoring logic (vibration, temperature trending) to OT system health and integrity monitoring.

rows.title: Potentially adverse events are analyzed to better understand associated activities
rows.vesselContext: Root-cause analysis of a cyber anomaly should follow the same investigation discipline as any other hazardous occurrence, feeding the same trend log.

rows.title: The incident response plan is executed once an incident is declared
rows.vesselContext: A cyber incident should trigger the same drilled emergency-response muscle memory as fire or flooding — the "Respond" step, operationalized through existing drill discipline rather than a separate cyber-only plan nobody rehearses.

rows.title: Internal and external stakeholders are notified of incidents
ism: Section 3 (Company Responsibilities — reporting to flag state/class)
rows.vesselContext: Who gets called — DPA, flag state, class society, insurer — during a cyber incident should be pre-defined exactly like any other emergency contact tree, not improvised.

rows.title: Analysis is performed to determine what took place during an incident and its root cause
rows.vesselContext: Post-incident cyber analysis should feed the same non-conformity trend review the Company already conducts at management review, not a parallel unread IT report.

rows.title: The recovery portion of the incident response plan is executed once initiated
rows.msc: No dedicated MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 clause — "Recover" is the least-developed step in current maritime guidance
rows.relationship: partial — clearest gap in the whole crosswalk
rows.vesselContext: Backup-ECDIS and OT-rebuild procedures are rarely drilled with the rigor of lifeboat or fire drills. CSF 2.0's Recover function is the single biggest gap versus current ISM/IMO practice.

rows.title: Recovery activities and progress are communicated to internal and external stakeholders
rows.vesselContext: Stakeholder communication during recovery (charterers, flag state, class, insurer) needs the same discipline as initial incident notification — often forgotten once the immediate emergency passes.
